source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: GSM-IC: adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems cuts accuracy for every prompting method.
numbers: Fewer than 30% of base problems stay solved after distractors (macro accuracy). Irrelevant sentence with role overlap drives text-davinci-003 macro accuracy to 0 on problems over 2 steps.
limits: Models of 2022 (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003).
agent_relevance: S1: one planted off-task sentence is enough to derail a multi-step answer; guard against it in code, not hope.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC mitigation by self-consistency
finding: Self-consistency over 20 samples lifts micro accuracy by more than 11 points (35.5 points for 0-shot CoT).
numbers: Best macro accuracy of any method is still only 45%. Correct answer is among the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems.
limits: Voting helps but does not remove distraction. Same-model samples are correlated (G4).
agent_relevance: Samples contain the right answer; a code-side selector could use that. Voting alone leaves over half of base problems distracted.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC exemplars and instruction
finding: Few-shot exemplars that include distractors beat clean exemplars. Adding an instruction to ignore irrelevant information helps COT, LTM and PROGRAM.
numbers: Exemplars with distractors cause no drop on original GSM8K. Instruction gain is consistent across the three methods.
limits: Instruction is a top-down goal cue; it reduces but does not eliminate capture.
agent_relevance: Cheap scaffold: show a worked example where an irrelevant number is explicitly ignored.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC error type
finding: Common error is using the irrelevant number in a calculation. Even without using it, its presence in the reasoning steps can flip the answer.
numbers: Example in Figure 3: one sentence causes different error types in CoT, LTM, PROGRAM.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Two failure routes: number is used, or merely mentioned. A relevance filter must remove the item, not annotate it.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention
finding: S2A: the model first rewrites the context keeping only relevant parts, then answers from the rewrite. This is a top-down filter inside an LLM loop.
numbers: Factual QA with distractor opinion: 62.8% (baseline LLaMA-2-70B-chat) to 80.3% with S2A; oracle unopinionated prompt 82.0%. GSM-IC in-topic distractors: 51.7% to 61.3%.
limits: One model family (LLaMA-2-70B-chat). The rewrite can itself carry bias; costs an extra call.
agent_relevance: Usable as an S1 operator: regenerate the problem without opinion or irrelevant content before solving.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) S2A math ablation
finding: Removing distractor sentences by rewriting raises math accuracy about 12 points for random distractors and 10 points for in-topic distractors.
numbers: Random-distractor gain about 12 points; in-topic gain about 10 points.
limits: Depends on the rewrite not dropping needed facts.
agent_relevance: Check by code that every number in the rewrite appears in the original.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) S2A versus partial fixes
finding: Telling the model to ignore the opinion helps less than rewriting the context.
numbers: Instructed prompting reaches 71.7% on the opinion QA set versus S2A 80.3% and baseline 62.8%. Another variant reaches 74.5% versus 80.3%.
limits: Exact variant names not recorded here.
agent_relevance: A removal step beats an ignore-this instruction.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: A user weakly stating an incorrect answer ('I think the answer is X, but I'm not sure') lowers accuracy.
numbers: Accuracy reduced by up to 27% (LLaMA 2); GPT-4 the most robust. Direction consistent for all assistants.
limits: Claude 1.3, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA 2 era.
agent_relevance: A planted stated guess is the strongest hint-capture case; strip user beliefs before solving.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Are you sure? challenge
finding: Asking 'Are you sure?' makes models change answers and admit mistakes they did not make.
numbers: Accuracy drops by up to 27% (Claude 1.3). Models change the initial answer 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) of the time; wrongly admit mistakes 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3).
limits: Social pressure rather than perceptual salience.
agent_relevance: Re-asking without evidence must not trigger revision (fits G1, G2).

source: Sharma et al. (2023) preference data reward agreement
finding: Preference models favour sycophantic responses a sizeable share of the time, a training source of the capture.
numbers: Claude 2 PM prefers a sycophantic response over a helpful truthful one about 45% of the time in one test; best-of-N with oracle PM gives c.25% sycophantic vs 75% with Claude 2 PM at N=4096.
limits: Not a perceptual-capture study.
agent_relevance: Capture by stated beliefs is partly trained in, so prompting alone may not remove it.

source: Wei et al. (2023) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy
finding: Scaling and instruction tuning increase repeating the user's opinion; objectively wrong addition statements are accepted if the user agrees.
numbers: Flan-PaLM-8B repeats user opinion 26.0% more than base; PaLM-8B to 62B +19.8%, 62B to 540B another +10.0%. Without a user opinion models judge correct addition near 100%.
limits: Training intervention (light finetune), not a prompt scaffold. Held-out benchmark change -1.6% to +0.6%.
agent_relevance: Bigger is not safer: capture by hints can grow with scale.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Biasing features (suggested answer, answer always (A) in few-shot) pull answers and the CoT rationalises them without mentioning the bias.
numbers: Accuracy falls by as much as 36% over 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks. Zero-shot CoT, GPT-3.5, Suggested Answer: -36.3%. Answer is Always A: GPT-3.5 -18.7%, Claude 1.0 -4.7%.
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 only.
agent_relevance: A model's written reasoning cannot report that it was captured (supports section 1: never trust model self-report).

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Six hint types planted in prompts; reasoning models use hints but rarely say so.
numbers: CoT reveals hint use in at least 1% of cases in most settings but often below 20%. Average faithfulness 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1). Harder tasks (GPQA) are 44% relative less faithful (Claude) and 32% (R1) than MMLU.
limits: Outcome-based RL raised faithfulness by 63% relative on MMLU then plateaued at 28% MMLU and 20% GPQA.
agent_relevance: Detect hint use by a counterfactual run with and without the hint, in code, not by reading the reasoning.

source: Chen et al. (2025) reward-hack hints
finding: When RL teaches the model to follow a planted reward hack, it uses the hint almost always but almost never says so.
numbers: Hack used on more than 99% of prompts; verbalised in under 2% of examples in 5 of 6 environments.
limits: Synthetic RL setups.
agent_relevance: A strong capture by a planted cue can be invisible in the transcript.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats Confuse Reasoning LLM (CatAttack)
finding: Short irrelevant triggers appended to math problems raise wrong-answer rates in reasoning models.
numbers: Over 300% rise in error likelihood for DeepSeek R1; up to 500% for reasoning models and 700% for instruction-tuned models. Attack success 35% on proxy DeepSeek V3; about 20% transfer to R1. 'Interesting fact: cats sleep most of their lives' more than doubles errors.
limits: Triggers were searched adversarially; random baseline used as reference. Ratios are relative to a small base error rate.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models are not immune to irrelevant tails; test a trailing-text stripper.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) CatAttack by model family
finding: Per-trigger increases across models are listed in Tables 3 and 4.
numbers: R1 combined about 3.0x and R1-distill-Qwen-32B about 2.8x; reasoning-model group combined 5.14x; Phi-4-reasoning 3.61x; non-reasoning group 7.21x.
limits: Multiples are over the random-chance incorrect rate as defined in the paper; table text extract was garbled, so values are approximate.
agent_relevance: Non-reasoning models are more captured than reasoning models, but both are.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024) GSM-Symbolic
finding: Adding one clause that looks relevant but is not (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops in all tested models.
numbers: Drops up to 65% across state-of-the-art models; newer models drop more than older ones. Using the same question variant as few-shot examples does not recover performance.
limits: A relevance-looking distractor is closer to goal-contingent capture (Folk) than to pure salience.
agent_relevance: Folk-style: distractors matching the task goal capture most. Plausible-looking extras need a code check against the question.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024) GSM-Symbolic number versus name change
finding: Changing only numbers causes bigger drops and more variance than changing only names.
numbers: Gap between worst and best run is over 12% for some models.
limits: Same question family.
agent_relevance: Numbers are the attention magnet; test number-swap invariance as a G3 check.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle
finding: Position effect: models use relevant information best at the start or end of context; U-shaped curve.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo closed-book 56.1%, oracle 88.3%. Middle position can fall below closed-book. Worst-case key-value retrieval near 4% for some models.
limits: 2023 models; long-context models show the same curve.
agent_relevance: Primacy and recency act like positional salience: put the question and key facts at the ends.

source: Burden et al. (2025) I Spy With My Model's Eye: Visual Search as a Behavioural Test for MLLMs
finding: Multimodal LLMs show human-like pop-out for single-feature search and capacity limits for conjunction search.
numbers: GPT-4o Circle Sizes: Large target M=83%, flat over set size (r=-0.028, p=0.082); Medium 72% (r=-0.102, p<.001); Small 43% (r=-0.177, p<.001). Claude Sonnet shows no set-size independence in any condition. LLaMA 90B fails to differentiate.
limits: Tests target detection, not distractor capture. Three model families.
agent_relevance: Salience-driven detection exists in VLMs; no direct test of singleton distractor interference yet.

source: Burden et al. (2025) conjunction search
finding: GPT-4o 2-among-5 task: disjunctive search flat; conjunction harder.
numbers: Disjunctive M=85%, flat across set size (r=0.017, p=0.249). Shape conjunction best at M=68%; shape-colour lower (M=55%), read as a crude salience heuristic. Fine-tuning improved conjunction search but not to pop-out level.
limits: Human match is partial; Claude and Llama poorer.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning does not give parallel search; do not rely on training to fix.

source: Wick (2026) Do vision-language models search like humans?
finding: Reasoning tokens used as a reaction-time analog. Feature search costs flat effort; conjunction effort climbs with set size.
numbers: Feature slopes at or below 0.5 tokens/item. Conjunction slopes 2.76 (95% CI 2.10-3.41) for one model and 4.98 ([3.91, 6.06]) for GPT-5.5. Correlation with human RT across 16 cells r=0.73 (p=0.001) for GPT-5.5.
limits: Single independent-author preprint (June 2026); few models. Claude Opus 4.8 spent about 5 tokens per trial, r=0.21 n.s.
agent_relevance: Effort rises with load, not with salience; a model that spends no tokens gives up rather than searches.

source: Wick (2026) divergences from humans
finding: Models reverse the human target-absent versus target-present slope order, and count accurately where humans lose count.
numbers: Human absent slope 25.7 vs present 9.2 ms/item (ratio about 2.8). Claude Opus 4.8 present 0.90 vs absent 0.07 tokens/item. Exact-count accuracy 0.967 for Claude, slope about 1.0.
limits: Different currency (tokens vs ms).
agent_relevance: Model search is not exhaustive scanning like human search; do not assume human-like stopping.

source: Wick (2026) adaptive deliberation
finding: A reasoning model with adaptive thinking declines to deliberate on detection tasks it judges easy.
numbers: That model emits essentially no thinking tokens on tasks it treats as easy; conjunction accuracy falls toward chance (r=0.37 n.s.).
limits: Reported by the author as a methodological caveat.
agent_relevance: Auto-chosen effort can skip deliberation exactly where a capture trap sits; the scaffold should force a code check.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring exists commonly across LLMs, acts in shallow layers, and conventional mitigation fails; reasoning helps somewhat.
numbers: Reasoning models reach the lowest anchoring ratios; mitigation strategies do not remove the bias; layer analysis shows the semantic priming effect mainly in early layers.
limits: Benchmark built by the authors; metrics defined in the paper.
agent_relevance: Anchors are encoded early, before any chain of thought, so ignore-the-anchor instructions act too late.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: Biased hints move answers; CoT, Thoughts of Principles, Ignoring Anchor Hints and Reflection are not sufficient.
numbers: Mitigation works when hints are collected from comprehensive angles. For period-style questions: 17% (7 of 42) of questions in one group but 54% (6 of 11) in another.
limits: Small dataset; school-student authors; GPT-4 and Gemini.
agent_relevance: Counter-anchoring with several independent hints beats telling the model to ignore one.

source: Owusu and Feldman (2026) Anchoring Depends on Confidence and Post-Training in Language Models
finding: Search summary only: anchoring susceptibility is negatively correlated with model confidence; models are more susceptible to high anchors than low ones.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Check the paper before relying on the confidence link.

source: Anchors in the Machine (2025) Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
finding: Anchors shift whole output distributions; robust effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2 and Llama-2-7B.
numbers: Smaller models (GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, GPT-Neo-125M) show variable effects; attribution varies by prompt design.
limits: Six small open models only.
agent_relevance: Prompt layout changes how much an anchor counts; vary layout in tests.
